name: Sample proportion (single group)
expression: p_i = x_i / n_i ;  pi_hat = p
variables: x_i = number of cases (people with the condition) in study i; n_i = total sample size of study i; p_i = sample proportion (prevalence); pi = population proportion.
notes: Worked: 48/80 = 0.60. effect_sizes.proportion('PR', x, n) returns (p, p(1-p)/n, note). The engine adds 0.5 to x and 1 to n only when x = 0 or x = n (cc_to='only0'); the book uses no correction. The book's Table 6.2 enters rounded p values (Fichter 0.75 for 5/7, Shen 0.512 for 154/300); compute from counts.

name: Variance and SE of a sample proportion
expression: Var(p_i) = p_i (1 - p_i) / n_i ;  SE(p_i) = sqrt(Var(p_i)) ;  w_i = 1 / Var(p_i)
variables: p_i = sample proportion; n_i = sample size; Var = sampling variance; SE = standard error; w_i = inverse-variance weight.
notes: Worked: p = 0.60, n = 80 gives Var = 0.003, SE = 0.054772. Zero when p = 0 or 1 (infinite weight); the source does not address this.

name: Normal approximation of the sample proportion
expression: p ~ N( mu(p) = pi , Var(p) = pi (1 - pi) / n )   for 'large' n (book: usually n >= 30)
variables: p = sample proportion; pi = population proportion; n = sample size; N = normal distribution.
notes: The book uses this to argue that no transformation is needed. Debatable: adequacy also depends on n·p and n·(1 − p) (rule of thumb ≥ 5–10, external), not on n alone.

name: Wald confidence interval for a single estimate
expression: LL = theta_hat - z_{alpha/2} * SE(theta_hat) ;  UL = theta_hat + z_{alpha/2} * SE(theta_hat)
variables: theta_hat = study estimate (p or RD); SE = its standard error; z_{alpha/2} = upper alpha/2 point of N(0,1) (1.96 for 95%); LL, UL = lower and upper limits.

name: z test of a single or pooled estimate against zero
expression: Z = (theta_hat - 0) / SE(theta_hat) ;  P = P(|Z| > |z0|) = 2 * P(Z > |z0|)
variables: theta_hat = estimate (p, RD, or pooled theta_FE / theta_RE / theta_IVhet); SE = its standard error; z0 = observed value; Z ~ N(0,1) under H0: theta = 0; P = two-sided P value.
notes: Worked: 0.6/0.0548 = 10.949 [Ex 6.3]; −0.2/0.0727 = −2.75, P = 0.006 [Ex 7.3]. For a prevalence the test of pi = 0 is uninformative. The book takes P from normal tables (e.g. 0.0204 for |z| = 2.32; exact for z = −2.31725 is 0.0205) and prints very small P as 0.

name: Two-proportion effect-size parameters (RD, OR, RR)
expression: theta_1 = pi_1 - pi_2 (RD) ;  theta_2 = [pi_1/(1 - pi_1)] / [pi_2/(1 - pi_2)] (OR) ;  theta_3 = pi_1 / pi_2 (RR)
variables: pi_1, pi_2 = population proportions (risks) in the treatment and control groups.
notes: Estimated by plugging in the sample proportions p_1, p_2. Ch 7 analyses only the RD; OR and RR variances are in Chs 4–5. effect_sizes.two_by_two(measure, e1, n1, e2, n2) takes events and arm totals.

name: Sample log odds ratio and log risk ratio
variables: p_1, p_2 = sample proportions in the treatment and control groups (independent samples of sizes n_1, n_2).
notes: Only defined here; variances and pooling are in Chs 4–5. The engine returns ln OR / ln RR with their variances and applies a 0.5 continuity correction only for zero cells.

name: Risk difference and its variance
expression: RD = theta_hat = p_1 - p_2 ;  Var(RD) = p_1 (1 - p_1)/n_1 + p_2 (1 - p_2)/n_2 ;  SE(RD) = sqrt(Var(RD))
variables: p_1 = events/patients in group 1 (treatment); p_2 = events/patients in group 2 (control); n_1, n_2 = group sizes.
notes: Worked: p_1 = 0.60 (n_1 = 80), p_2 = 0.80 (n_2 = 70): RD = −0.20, Var = 0.0052857 (source misprints 0.5285), SE = 0.0727. Sign convention: negative RD = lower risk on treatment. effect_sizes.two_by_two('RD', ...) uses the uncorrected RD and adds a 0.5 correction to the variance only when it would otherwise be 0 (both arms 0% or 100%); the book has no zero cells.

name: Fixed-effect (inverse-variance) pooled estimate
expression: theta_FE = sum_i w_i theta_i / sum_i w_i ,  w_i = 1 / v_i
variables: theta_i = study estimate (p_i in Ch 6, RD_i in Ch 7); v_i = within-study variance; w_i = inverse-variance weight; k = number of studies (sums over i = 1..k).
notes: Call models.meta_analysis(yi, vi, model='fixed', ci_method='z'). Worked: 13244/22509 = 0.5884 (schizophrenia); −769.624/57295 = −0.01343 (aspirin RD). MetaXL model 'IV'.

name: Variance and SE of the fixed-effect estimate
expression: Var(theta_FE) = 1 / sum_i w_i ;  SE(theta_FE) = sqrt(1 / sum_i w_i)
variables: w_i = 1/v_i = inverse-variance weight of study i.

name: z-based confidence interval and test for a pooled estimate
expression: LL, UL = theta_M -/+ z_{alpha/2} * SE(theta_M) ;  Z = theta_M / SE(theta_M) ;  reject H0 if |z0| >= z_{alpha/2} or P <= alpha
variables: theta_M = pooled estimate under model M (FE, RE or IVhet); SE(theta_M) = its standard error; z_{alpha/2} = 1.96 for 95%.
notes: All CIs in the chapters are z-based (no t, no HKSJ). The engine's default for random effects is HKSJ, so pass ci_method='z' to reproduce. Worked FE CIs: (0.57, 0.60) [lower 0.5753 truncated]; (−0.0216, −0.0052).

name: Study weight percentage
expression: %W_i = 100 * w_i / sum_j w_j   (FE and IVhet) ;   %W_i* = 100 * w_i* / sum_j w_j*   (RE)
variables: w_i = 1/v_i (FE/IVhet weight); w_i* = 1/(v_i + tau^2) (RE weight).
notes: Returned as weights_pct. FE and IVhet weights are identical by construction. Worked MetaXL: Babigian 61.8% (FE) vs 24.0% (RE); ISIS-2 48.5% (FE) vs 28.3% (RE). A subgroup's weight share is the sum of its studies' % weights (67.6% vs 32.4% in Fig. 6.4).

name: Cochran's Q (computational form)
expression: Q = sum_i w_i theta_i^2 - (sum_i w_i theta_i)^2 / sum_i w_i  =  sum_i w_i (theta_i - theta_FE)^2
variables: w_i = 1/v_i; theta_i = study estimate; theta_FE = fixed-effect pooled estimate; k = number of studies.
notes: Worked: 7873.8 − 13244²/22509 printed as 81.4430 (from unrounded sums; the rounded sums give 81.20); 20.7597 − (−769.624)²/57295 = 10.4216. Use the deviation form at full precision. With exact x/n instead of the book's rounded p the schizophrenia Q is 80.02; MetaXL (transformed scale) prints 80.18.

name: P value of Cochran's Q
expression: P = Pr( chi^2_{k-1} > Q )
variables: Q = Cochran's Q; k − 1 = degrees of freedom; chi^2_{k-1} = chi-square distribution with k − 1 df.
notes: The book reads P from a chi-square table: chi^2_{5, 0.001} = 20.515 (so Q = 81.44 gives P < 0.001) and chi^2_{6, 0.10} = 10.6446 (so Q = 10.42 gives P > 0.10; exact 0.108, MetaXL 0.11).

name: I^2 statistic
expression: I^2 = (Q - df) / Q * 100% ,  df = k - 1 ;  truncated: I^2 = max(0, (Q - df)/Q) * 100%
variables: Q = Cochran's Q; df = k − 1; k = number of studies.
notes: Worked: (81.44 − 5)/81.44 = 93.86% (printed '93.86 × 100%'); (10.42 − 6)/10.42 = 42.4%. Truncation at 0 is not stated in the chapters; MetaXL prints 0% when Q < df.

name: DerSimonian–Laird scaling constant C
expression: C = sum_i w_i - sum_i w_i^2 / sum_i w_i
variables: w_i = 1/v_i = fixed-effect weight of study i.
notes: Returned as key 'C' by models.heterogeneity. Worked: 22509.028 − 234606499.3/22509.028 = 12086.25; 57295 − 991686133/57295 printed 39986.25 (exact from counts 39986.252; the rounded sums give 39986.58).

name: DerSimonian–Laird between-study variance
expression: tau^2_DL = (Q - df) / C ;  truncated: tau^2_DL = max(0, (Q - df) / C)
variables: Q = Cochran's Q; df = k − 1; C = sum w_i − sum w_i^2 / sum w_i.
notes: Book calls it 'scaled excess variation'; truncation at 0 is not stated. Worked: (81.44304 − 5)/12086.25 = 0.006325; (10.4216 − 6)/39986.25 = 0.000111 (exact 0.00011058). The book rounds tau^2 before computing weights. [note: Cochrane Handbook v6 prefers REML or Paule–Mandel; models.tau2_reml / models.tau2_pm are available.]

name: Random-effects weights
expression: v_i* = v_i + tau^2 ;  w_i* = 1 / (v_i + tau_hat^2)
variables: v_i = within-study variance; tau_hat^2 = estimated between-study variance (DL); w_i* = random-effects weight.
notes: Use models.meta_analysis(yi, vi, model='random', tau2_method='DL', ci_method='z'). Worked first rows: Bondestam 1/(0.024 + 0.006325) = 32.976; MRC-1 2605.4.

name: Random-effects pooled estimate and SE
expression: theta_RE = sum_i w_i* theta_i / sum_i w_i* ;  SE(theta_RE) = sqrt(1 / sum_i w_i*)
variables: w_i* = 1/(v_i + tau_hat^2); theta_i = study estimate.
notes: Worked: 386.0286/655.4021 = 0.58899, SE = 0.039061 (the DOCX shows the fraction inverted); −359.393/24054 = −0.0149, SE = 0.006448, CI (−0.02758, −0.0023), P = 0.0204 (normal table; exact 0.0205 for the book's z = −2.31725, 0.0204 at full precision). CI/test are z-based. [note: Cochrane Handbook v6 suggests considering HKSJ (t-based) CIs and a prediction interval for random effects; a z-based DL CI can be too narrow when k is small.]

name: IVhet pooled estimate
expression: theta_IVhet = sum_i w_i theta_i / sum_i w_i  ( = theta_FE ),  w_i = 1 / v_i
variables: theta_i = study estimate; v_i = within-study variance; w_i = fixed-effect weight.
notes: Doi et al. (2015a). Call via models.meta_analysis(yi, vi, model='ivhet'), which dispatches to models._ivhet. The Ch 6 estimate is misprinted once as 0.5889 (13243.84/22509 = 0.5884). [note: IVhet is proposed and promoted mainly by its developers (Doi, Barendregt, Khan and colleagues); Cochrane Handbook v6 does not use it.]

name: IVhet variance and SE
expression: Var(theta_IVhet) = sum_i [ (w_i / sum_j w_j)^2 * (v_i + tau_hat^2) ] ;  SE = sqrt(Var(theta_IVhet))
variables: w_i = 1/v_i; v_i = within-study variance; tau_hat^2 = DerSimonian–Laird between-study variance.
notes: The per-study term (w_i/sum w)^2 (v_i + tau^2) is labelled 'V*' (Table 6.4) or 'W*' (Table 7.4) but is a variance component, not a weight. Worked: Var = 0.002973, SE = 0.054527 (schizophrenia); Var = 0.00005099, SE = 0.00714 (aspirin; 5.086e-5 with unrounded tau^2). CI and test z-based; the IVhet upper-limit formula on p. 153 misprints '−1.96' for '+1.96'. [note: an author-group proposal (Doi et al. 2015a), not part of Cochrane guidance, which uses random effects with REML or Paule–Mandel τ².]

name: Logit transformation of a proportion [external]
expression: y_i = ln( x_i / (n_i - x_i) ) ;  v_i = 1/x_i + 1/(n_i - x_i) ;  back-transform p = exp(y) / (1 + exp(y))
variables: x_i = cases; n_i = sample size; y_i = logit proportion; v_i = its approximate variance.
locator: Not in source (Ch6 pp. 119–136 use raw proportions)
notes: [external] Not derived in Khan Ch 6. Engine: effect_sizes.proportion('PLO', x, n) and effect_sizes.back_transform('PLO', value). Needs a continuity correction (commonly 0.5 added to x and n − x) when x = 0 or x = n; the engine adds 0.5 to x and 1 to n in that case.

name: Freeman–Tukey double arcsine transformation (MetaXL convention) [external]
expression: t_i = asin( sqrt( x_i / (n_i + 1) ) ) + asin( sqrt( (x_i + 1) / (n_i + 1) ) ) ;  v_i = 1 / (n_i + 0.5)
variables: x_i = cases; n_i = sample size; t_i = double-arcsine transformed proportion (MetaXL/Barendregt scale); v_i = its variance.
locator: Ch6 App. A6.2 p. 136 (Stata ftt); Figs. 6.1–6.4 pp. 126–134 (reconstruction)
notes: [external; inferred from the book's MetaXL output, not stated] Reproduces MetaXL FE weights (0.2, 5.6, 26.6, 61.8, 0.1, 5.7) and, with x_i = printed p_i × N_i, Q = 80.18 and all study rows; integer counts give Q = 78.99. The engine (effect_sizes.proportion('PFT', x, n)) uses the metafor half scale: y = t/2, v = 1/(4n + 2) = (1/4)·1/(n + 0.5); weights, Q, I^2 and back-transformed results are identical, but tau^2 and SE differ by factors 4 and 2. No continuity correction needed for x = 0 or x = n. [note: the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine is contested. Its back-transformation depends on the n chosen and can give misleading pooled proportions when study sizes differ widely (Schwarzer et al. 2019, Res Synth Methods). Current guidance prefers a binomial GLMM (random-intercept logistic model) or the logit scale, and keeps FT as a sensitivity analysis at most.]

name: Miller (1978) inverse of the Freeman–Tukey double arcsine [external]
expression: p = 0.5 * [ 1 - sgn(cos t) * sqrt( 1 - ( sin t + (sin t - 1/sin t) / m )^2 ) ]
variables: t = value on the double-arcsine (MetaXL) scale; m = sample-size parameter of the inverse; sgn = sign function.
notes: [external] MetaXL output in the book is reproduced with m = n_i + 0.5 for a study and m = 1/Var(pooled t) for the pooled estimate and each CI limit. Engine: effect_sizes.pft_inverse(y, n) takes y = t/2 (it uses sin 2y, cos 2y) and n = m; effect_sizes.back_transform('PFT', value, n_harmonic) and the pipeline default to the harmonic mean of n_i, which gives FE (0.58, 0.60) instead of MetaXL's (0.57, 0.60). To mimic MetaXL pass m = 1/Var(pooled t) = 1/(4·Var(pooled y)). [note: the dependence on m is the main criticism of this inverse (Schwarzer et al. 2019); report the m used, or prefer a GLMM or logit analysis.]

name: Test of subgroup differences under the fixed-effect model [derived]
expression: Q_between = Q_total - sum_g Q_within,g ;  df = G - 1 ;  P = Pr(chi^2_{G-1} > Q_between)
variables: Q_total = Cochran's Q over all studies; Q_within,g = Q within subgroup g; G = number of subgroups.
notes: [derived, not printed in the source] From MetaXL: 80.18 − 6.29 − 0.48 ≈ 73.4 on 1 df. moderators.subgroup_analysis computes Q_between = sum_g w_g (mu_g − mu_bar)^2 with w_g = 1/SE_g^2, which equals the partition above under FE (model='fixed').

name: Absolute effect per 1000 from a risk difference
expression: events prevented per 1000 = -1000 * RD   (RD = p_treatment - p_control)
variables: RD = pooled risk difference (treatment minus control).
notes: Derived for interpretation (not printed): RD −0.013 (FE) to −0.015 (RE) ≈ 13–15 fewer deaths per 1000 treated with aspirin. Report with the CI limits converted the same way.
